blocks.text: **The problem.** Implement a last-in-first-out **stack** using only **two queues**. Your class `MyStack` must support `push(x)`, `pop()` (remove and return the top), `top()` (return the top) and `empty()`. You may only use standard queue operations: add to the **back**, remove from the **front**, look at the front, size and is-empty. `pop` and `top` are only called when the stack isn't empty.

blocks.alt: The mismatch. After pushing 1, 2, 3, a stack must hand back 3 first. A queue holding 1, 2, 3 can only hand back 1, the oldest, from its front.

blocks.text: A queue only ever releases its **oldest** item; a stack must release its **newest**. Every solution has to dig the newest item out of the back of a queue — the only question is **when** to do the digging, at pop time or at push time.

In JavaScript each queue below is a plain array used only with `push` (add at the back) and `shift` (remove from the front), so the queue operations are easy to see. `shift` is itself O(n) on large arrays; as the problem intends, we count **queue operations**.
1. Brute force: dig at pop time, and again for top

Push is just an enqueue on `q1`. To pop, the newest item is at the **back**, so move every other item into the helper `q2`, take the one left over, then swap the queues' names. `top()` has no shortcut: it pops the top and pushes it straight back.

blocks.alt: Popping from q1 holding 1, 2, 3: the first two items, 1 and 2, move to q2 in order; 3 is left alone and is returned. Then q2 becomes the main queue.

blocks.text: **push O(1); pop and top O(n); space O(n).** Every pop **and** every peek shuffles the whole queue.

`top()` shouldn't have to dig. The top is simply the **newest** item, so store it in a variable `topVal` whenever we push. Pop still digs, but while it moves items into `q2` it can update `topVal` for free: the **last** item it moves is the next-newest, which becomes the new top.

blocks.alt: Popping from q1 holding 1, 2, 3 with topVal = 3. 1 and then 2 move to q2, and topVal is set to each as it moves, so it ends as 2, the last one moved. 3 is returned, and 2 is now the top.

elements.text: 2 was moved last: the new top
elements.originalText: 2 was moved last: the new top

blocks.text: **push and top O(1); pop O(n); space O(n).** (When the last item is popped, `topVal` goes stale — harmless, because `top()` is never called on an empty stack.)
3. Best solution: dig at push time instead

Flip where the work goes. Keep `q1` in **newest-first** order at all times, so its front **is** the top. To push `x`: put `x` into the **empty** `q2`, move everything from `q1` in behind it, then swap the names. Now `pop` and `top` are a plain dequeue and peek, with no variable to keep in sync.

blocks.alt: Pushing 4 when q1 holds 3, 2, 1 newest-first. 4 goes into the empty q2, then 3, 2 and 1 follow it, so q2 holds 4, 3, 2, 1. The queues swap names.

blocks.caption: Each push builds a fresh newest-first queue in q2, then the names swap.

blocks.text: **push O(n); pop, top and empty O(1); space O(n).**

blocks.alt: Brute force: pop & top O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: pop O(n) time, O(n) space. Best: push O(n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: Approaches 2 and 3 each leave exactly **one** operation at O(n). Approach 3 is the textbook answer: `q1` is always a ready-made stack, so the two reads, `pop` and `top`, are instant and there's no extra state to get wrong. If your program pushes far more often than it pops, approach 2 does less total work — say so in an interview, it shows you understand the trade.

items: **A single item** — push then pop: the moving loop runs zero times.
**top right after a pop** — `push 1, push 2, pop, top` must give 1. This is the case that breaks a badly updated `topVal`.
**Pop until empty, then push again** — `empty()` must flip back to false and the order must restart cleanly.
**Repeated values** — `push 5, push 5, pop, top` gives 5 and 5; the order still matters even when values match.
**Stack using a single queue** — the next problem: the second queue isn't needed at all.
**Queue using two stacks** — the mirror problem, with a cleverer trick that makes every operation O(1) amortized.
**Stack using a deque** — trivial: a deque already adds and removes at the same end in O(1).
**Min Stack** — a stack that also reports its smallest item in O(1).
